criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design; discusses the context of ethical issues in engineering organisations; identifies relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Identifies stakeholders and links the dilemma to engineering quality and business pressure in a growing tech industry. Ethical issues (end-user harm, professional responsibility) are named but only briefly described in the introduction. Context and stakeholders are present but not developed in depth, so it sits between Very good and Excellent.

evidence.quote: Rachel is a Quality Assurance Engineer at a large electronics company faced with an ethical dilemma
The relevant stakeholders in this scenario include Rachel, Rachel’s company, the chip contract company, the government health department

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions on the ethical issues; draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: The case against shipping is developed with EACE clauses and cases, but the case for shipping is shallow and tangential (Apple example). The discussion leans toward opinion ('Rachel may think'). No criteria are given for when a defective product could be shipped, and the recommendations address only Rachel and her company, not the health department or end-users.

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument that justifies the conclusion; the body follows a logical structure, with linked paragraphs and content ordered to support the argument; arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: Sections follow a logical order (introduction, discussion, trade-off, conclusion), but the argument is undermined by its own recommendations. The conclusion says not to ship, while recommendation 1 says to accept the contract and recommendation 3 proposes delayed launches. This contradiction means the conclusion is not clearly supported by the arguments.

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence; research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Uses four references, including relevant external cases (NHS IT failures, Volkswagen) and the EACE code. Quantitative evidence is limited to an unsourced hypothetical. The Apple/CNBC source does not support the competitive claim well. The VW description is factually wrong, and references [3] and [4] are incomplete or garbled, so research depth is only moderate.

technical_issues.issue: Volkswagen case misdescribed: the defeat devices manipulated emissions tests on diesel vehicles, not crash-safety tests on electric vehicles.
Recommendation 1 (accept the contract) and recommendation 3 (delay launches) conflict with the conclusion that not shipping is the most ethical path and with the stated 'Not Ship' decision.
Reference [3] lacks author and URL; reference [4] has a garbled author and the URL is malformed in [1]; formatting is inconsistent.

overall: A competent ethics report with relevant stakeholders, a reasonable NHS case study and EACE links. Weaknesses include a missing abstract, no visuals, thin research, a factual error on Volkswagen, and recommendations that contradict the conclusion. No criteria are given for when shipping might be acceptable.

feedback.summary: You have written a competent ethics report that identifies key stakeholders, including Rachel, her company, the contract client, the health department and end-users, and links the dilemma to engineering quality. Your NHS and Volkswagen case studies give useful grounding. The main priorities are resolving the contradiction between your conclusion and recommendations, correcting the Volkswagen account, and adding an abstract and visual elements to strengthen the report's overall impact.
next_steps: Rewrite your recommendations so they follow from your conclusion that not shipping is most ethical, and set out a recommendation for each stakeholder, including the health department and end-users.

Correct the Volkswagen description so it refers to defeat devices manipulating emissions tests on diesel vehicles, and flag your 1% failure figure as a hypothetical assumption, ideally supported by a sourced failure rate.
Add an abstract of about 150 words and at least one visual, such as a decision table or stakeholder map, and check that every reference has complete authors and a working URL.

criteria.C1: You identify a clear set of stakeholders and link the dilemma to engineering quality and business pressure, which is a strong start. To reach Excellent, describe each ethical issue, such as end-user harm and professional responsibility, in more depth and explain why it matters in engineering design. Develop how organisational context, such as commercial pressure and quality governance, shapes each stakeholder's interests.
criteria.C2: Your case against shipping is developed with reference to the EACE code and external cases, giving your discussion a solid base. The case for shipping is thin and relies mainly on the Apple example, and parts read as opinion. To reach Very good, give the arguments for and against equal depth and objective support, then draw conclusions on how each stakeholder, not just Rachel, should decide.
criteria.C3: Your sections follow a logical order from introduction to discussion to conclusion. However, your recommendations to accept the contract and delay launches contradict your conclusion, which weakens the argument. To reach Very good, make every recommendation follow from your arguments so the conclusion is clearly supported and the case feels compelling to the reader.
criteria.C4: You draw on four references, including relevant NHS and Volkswagen cases and the EACE code, which shows genuine research. To reach Very good, add quantitative and qualitative evidence, support the competitive-advantage claim with a source that directly addresses it, and state clearly that your failure rate is an assumption. Correct the Volkswagen facts and complete the incomplete references.
criteria.C5: Your report is organised into recognisable sections, but language errors, a missing abstract and the absence of figures or tables limit its clarity. To reach Very good, proofread carefully for grammar, typos and word choice, add a concise abstract, and include visual elements such as a table comparing shipping options. Format all references consistently and ensure each one directly supports an argument.
